Drinkers
drĭngk´ẽrz
n. pl. (those who drink; habitual takers of wine)
From drink, Saxon drincan. Joel addresses the word to a class of men and tells them to weep, because the locusts have taken away the thing their lives were organised around.

Biblical Definition

The prophet's first summons in the locust plague is to the men least likely to notice a national calamity: “Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth” (Joel 1:5). God reaches them through the loss of the very thing they loved; the supply fails, and the stupor breaks. The devastation is total and is described as an invading army: “For a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lion” (Joel 1:6). The purpose of the whole visitation is stated when the call to repentance comes: “Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning” (Joel 2:12). And the promise on the far side is the restoration of exactly what was eaten: “And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you” (Joel 2:25).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines drinker as one who drinks; chiefly, one who drinks spirituous liquors to excess; a drunkard.

expand to see more

DRINKER, n. One who drinks; chiefly, one who drinks spirituous liquors to excess; a drunkard; a tippler.

DRUNKARD, n. One given to ebriety or an excessive use of strong liquor; a person who habitually is drunk.

WINE, n. The fermented juice of grapes; in Scripture, both a blessing that cheereth God and man, and a mocker.

SOBRIETY, n. Habitual soberness or temperance; freedom from intoxication.

LOCUST, n. An insect which multiplies to an immense degree and devastates whole countries.

Key Scripture

Joel 1:5 — "Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth."

Joel 1:6 — "For a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lion."

Joel 2:12 — "Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning:"

Joel 2:25 — "And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you."

Modern Corruption

Drunkenness is treated purely as a disease to be managed, with no room left for the repentance Joel calls for, or else all use of wine is condemned against the plain text of Scripture.

expand to see more

Two errors bracket this subject. The first is total abstinence taught as a biblical requirement, which cannot be squared with a Bible in which wine maketh glad the heart of man, in which the Lord Jesus made a great quantity of it at a wedding and gave the cup at the supper, and in which Paul told Timothy to use a little for his stomach's sake. The dictionary holds Christian liberty here, with the warning Paul attaches to it about the weaker brother. The second error is the modern reflex that assigns drunkenness entirely to pathology, leaving the sufferer a patient and never a sinner — which removes the only door Joel offers, which is to turn to God with all the heart.

Scripture's own handling is neither. It names drunkenness as sin, lists it among the works of the flesh, and bars the drunkard from the kingdom in the same sentence as the covetous and the extortioner — and in the very next line tells the Corinthians that such were some of you, but ye are washed. It also recognises bondage: the drinkers of Joel 1 are asleep and have to be woken. The pastoral answer holds both, as the Reformed tradition has: real responsibility, real bondage, and a real deliverance that begins with the summons to awake and weep, and ends with the promise to restore the years the locust hath eaten.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shathah (H8354), to drink; shikkor (H7910), a drunkard; asis (H6071), new or sweet wine; shub (H7725), to turn, return.

expand to see more

Hebrew shathah (H8354) — to drink; drinkers of wine, Joel 1:5.

Hebrew shikkor (H7910) — a drunkard; the first class the prophet wakes.

Hebrew asis (H6071) — new wine, sweet wine; cut off from your mouth.

Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn, return; turn ye even to me with all your heart.

Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to make whole, restore; I will restore to you the years.

Usage

"“Howl, all ye drinkers of wine” — the first class Joel summons."

"“Turn ye even to me with all your heart” — the purpose of the plague."

"“I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten” — the promise beyond it."
